## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
There are no trials yet. The starting architecture scored 0.000 on both seeds, so both the network and the default recipe are suspect. The default budget is only about 131k steps, or 32 updates. Using fewer PPO epochs buys more fresh samples and more updates, which should matter on a task that streams new designs. On structure: a placement is right when every footprint cell is a missing target cell at the brick's landing layer, which is the highest build height under the footprint. That test needs layer-by-layer reasoning, plus local context for overhangs, where a brick that is too small can leave a cell with no support. The 2D trunk has to learn this test without help. This round has three candidates. (A) keeps the starting network and changes only the recipe. (B) adds a new network that scores each placement layer by layer, using the same recipe as A. (C) is B's network with one PPO epoch per update, to test whether more samples beat more epochs.

### Round 2
All three trials scored 0 on both seeds and also had 0 training success. That covers the baseline net with 2 epochs and the layer-by-layer head with 1 or 2 epochs. So neither more samples nor the layer-by-layer bias alone was enough. Two problems are likely: weak optimisation (too few sharp updates, and entropy keeping the policy spread over about 250 actions), and a placement head that cannot compare individual footprint cells. Min, max and average pooling lose which cell holds which height or target bit. Placing a brick correctly means comparing each cell's height and target occupancy at the landing layer, which pooling hides. This round separates the two causes. P1 changes only the baseline's recipe (1 epoch, higher lr, lower entropy). P2 gives each footprint cell its own input to an MLP head. P3 combines the two, so each pair of trials isolates one factor.

### Round 3
All six trials scored exactly 0 on both seeds, and success during training was also 0. That held across three head designs, including a layer-resolved head that matches the landing rule, and across recipes giving 1 to 2 epochs and 190k to 400k samples. So more data and better footprint pooling are not the missing piece. When very different networks fail this completely, something more basic is likely wrong. One candidate: the task warns that this world may not behave as described. Every network so far assumes action slot i lines up with grid cell i, through a per-cell convolutional head. If the action layout is permuted, transposed or shifted (for example, DONE placed first or footprints swapped), every such head would fail. This round tests that guess with heads that can learn any mapping from actions to cells: a dense flattened head added to the baseline (two recipes), and a transformer with learned position embeddings that can route any cell's information to any action slot. If all three score near 0, this guess is not the cause.

### Round 4
All 9 trials scored exactly 0 on both seeds, and training success was also 0. That held across recipes (1, 2 and 4 epochs; lr, entropy and gamma changes) and across heads (footprint pooling, layer-resolved, footprint-concat, dense, transformer). A policy that is merely weak should still build a few 6-brick designs exactly. A flat 0 instead suggests a structural mismatch: this world probably decodes actions differently from the stated layout. It might transpose or flip y and x, order actions cell-first instead of type-first, or put DONE first. Local convolutional heads cannot learn such a remapping. The dense and positional-transformer heads could learn it in principle, but probably too slowly with about 250k samples. So in this last round, every candidate scores several possible action layouts at once and sums them. Each layout gets its own small learned output map, so training can strengthen the correct one and shrink the others toward zero.
